title: NVIDIA Researchers Build AI Detector That Spots Fake Videos With Over 90% Accuracy in Milliseconds
excerpt: A new forensic-oriented approach from NVIDIA and university researchers can identify AI-generated videos across multiple generative models, even ones it has never seen before.
body:
• Researchers from NVIDIA and the University Federico II of Naples have developed a synthetic video detector that achieves over 91% accuracy across multiple AI video generators.
  • The system uses forensic-oriented data augmentation based on wavelet decomposition to identify low-level artifacts in AI-generated content, rather than relying on semantic flaws specific to one model.
  • The detector generalizes to video generators it was never trained on, including recent models like NOVA and FLUX, making it practical for real-world deployment.
  • The technology arrives as deepfake incidents surge globally, including a recent case where a fake Jensen Huang keynote attracted five times more YouTube viewers than the real one.

Beyond Face-Swaps

As AI-generated video becomes increasingly indistinguishable from reality, researchers at NVIDIA and the University Federico II of Naples have developed a new approach to synthetic video detection that works across generative models — including ones it has never encountered. The detector achieves over 91% average accuracy and processes footage fast enough for real-time applications, a meaningful step toward combating the rising tide of video deepfakes.

Unlike earlier detection systems that focused primarily on face-swapped videos or specific manipulation techniques, this approach targets the fundamental forensic artifacts left behind by generative architectures. The researchers identified that all AI video generators — whether diffusion-based, GAN-based, or autoencoder-based — leave subtle, low-level traces in their output that human eyes cannot see but AI classifiers can learn to detect.

How It Works

The system uses a forensic-oriented data augmentation strategy built on wavelet decomposition. Rather than learning to spot the high-level semantic flaws that characterize a specific model (like distorted fingers or inconsistent lighting), it focuses on frequency-domain artifacts shared across generative architectures. This design choice is critical: semantic flaws change as generators improve, but the underlying forensic traces persist.

The researchers trained their detector using data from a single generative model and tested it against videos from a wide range of other generators. Despite its simplicity, the approach achieved significant accuracy improvements over existing state-of-the-art detectors and maintained strong performance on very recent generative models, including NOVA and FLUX.

"A well-designed forensic classifier should focus on identifying intrinsic low-level artifacts introduced by a generative architecture rather than relying on high-level semantic flaws."

— NVIDIA and University Federico II of Naples research team

Why It Matters Now

The urgency is real. Deepfake technology has already caused high-profile incidents that illustrate the scale of the threat. In October 2025, a fake NVIDIA GTC keynote featuring a deepfaked Jensen Huang drew nearly 95,000 YouTube viewers — roughly five times the audience of the real event — while promoting a cryptocurrency scam. The fake was convincing enough to sit atop YouTube search results above the legitimate stream.

Such incidents are multiplying. Scammers have begun deploying deepfakes during live video conference calls to impersonate executives, and AI-generated political content has appeared across multiple election cycles. Existing platform moderation tools have struggled to keep pace with the quality of synthetic media.

The Indian Tech Connection

NVIDIA, led by CEO Jensen Huang, employs thousands of engineers across its operations, with a significant engineering presence in India. The company's AI research division has become one of the most prolific in the world, contributing to areas from autonomous driving to generative AI safety. The video detection work aligns with broader industry efforts to establish trust frameworks for AI-generated content, an area where Indian tech companies and researchers are playing an increasingly prominent role.

For newsrooms and media platforms — including outlets serving diaspora communities — reliable detection tools could help combat misinformation that often targets immigrant communities through manipulated videos of political leaders or fabricated news segments.
